lines.text: A destructor ties a struct's fields to its life.
Now: moving fields out one at a time, why a type with a destructor forbids it, and how a guard hands its buffer back to the pool anyway.
Here's the chapter's pipeline. Every message gets a sixty-four K buffer from a pool, and a guard should hand it back when the guard is dropped.
So inside drop, we try to move the buffer out. But there the guard is only borrowed, so it's refused: the move out of a borrow error.
The compiler suggests a clone. And it compiles... but a thousand full-size messages now cost a thousand and one allocations.
We wanted one.
By the end, you'll take fields out of structs and guards without a clone, fix the two move-out errors, and predict what every pattern binding does with ownership.
First the pipeline. Then why fields resist leaving. Then the free fix.
Here is the pipeline we will use for the rest of this topic, so learn its shape once.
One function fetches a buffer from the pool, and it is the only place a sixty four kibibyte buffer is ever allocated.
Follow the four stages. Fill borrows the buffer exclusively. Inspect borrows it to read a small header. Consume takes it and hands it back. And put returns it to the pool.
A thousand small messages cost one allocation, because every handover moves a thirty two byte value, an id and the vector's handle, never the payload.
Our subject is the last two stages, where the function owns the buffer.
Take one field out of the value. The buffer moves to a new owner. The value keeps a gap.
The heap data never moves. Only the buffer value does.
The header is a copy type, so reading it just copies.
But the frame as a whole is now partially moved. That's the use-after-move error, in its partial form.
Let's predict one.
A struct of three trace probes. One field has been moved out into a local.
At the closing brace, what gets dropped, and in what order?
Body first... it lives on in its new owner, declared last.
Then the struct drops what it still holds: head, then tail.
The hole drops nothing.
A hole can be filled again. Put a new value in, and the struct is whole.
It has to be declared mutable, and then you can move it as a unit.
Move a field on only one path, and the compiler keeps a drop flag for that one field.
At the brace, it checks the flag before dropping it. The other fields drop without a check.
Another prediction.
There are four ways. Each one takes a buffer out of something that holds it.

Only the box.
A vector index, a reference-counted pointer and a reference all reach the value through a borrow... and you can't move out through a borrow.
A box is the one kind of pointer that the language lets you move out of.
Now give the struct a destructor, and it's sealed.
The guard holds the pool, and the buffer in an option, which we'll explain soon. It returns the buffer when it drops.
Try to destructure the guard. You get the error about moving out of a type that implements drop.
Why? Drop borrows the whole value, exclusively, and may read every field. A field moved out early would hand it a hole.
Copy fields can still be read, because a copy moves nothing.

Through a borrow, you may never leave a hole.
The owner gets the value back when the loan ends.
It will read it, or drop it.
So moving a field out through an exclusive reference is refused. Even if you'd refill it on the very next line, a panic in between would hand the owner a hole.
That is the move out
of a borrow error.
The way out: replace it in one step.
Every one of these takes the value out and puts something back, in the same step.
Option take leaves none. Mem take leaves the default value. Mem replace leaves whatever you give it. And mem swap trades two places.
None of them allocates anything.
For collections, an owning removal avoids the hole another way: it shrinks the collection. Pop, swap remove, or drain.

Each stage hands a message's bytes to the writer by calling take, and then it returns the buffer to the pool.

Now we can solve the first problem.
Make already handed back a state the field can be in. The guard stores its buffer in an option.
At the brace, drop calls option take. The buffer goes to the pool, and none takes its place. No field is ever missing.
A thousand full-size messages... one allocation.
And here, the option costs no space at all.
The guard has a second way out: you can take the buffer out of it and use it yourself.
After that, the guard still reaches the end of its scope and its drop runs. What does the drop find?
Nothing to do.

The take left the guard's slot empty, so there is no buffer for the drop to put back. And because the take only borrows the field, it is not a move out of a type that has a destructor, which would be refused.
The caller owns the buffer now, and the guard has quietly stood down.

lines.text: This is where the guard earns its keep, on the error path.
Do it by hand and the put sits after the question mark, so every message that fails throws its buffer away, and the next message must allocate a fresh one.
Use the guard and the early return drops it, and its drop puts the buffer back. A hundred bad messages in a thousand cost one allocation, instead of a hundred.
The same holds if the code panics and unwinds. The only way to lose the buffer is a guard whose drop never runs, and that is safe, merely wasteful.
Three values each print a trace line when dropped, so we can watch the order. A pattern pulls out the tail, and the head is passed to the drop function.
Which runs first, and which last?
The head, then the tail, then the body.
The head goes the moment you hand it to drop, because that is a move into a function that ends it. Nothing else has left scope yet.
At the closing brace, the tail binding is dropped first, as a later declaration, and then the original struct, which now has only the body left.
A pattern is where ownership of the parts changes hands.
Each name in it either copies, moves, or borrows.
A plain name copies a copy type, and moves anything else.
Add ref, and that part is only borrowed. And an underscore touches nothing.
So destructuring the frame copies the header, moves the payload, and leaves the frame partially moved.
The guard's own drop does this. The buffer changes owner right there. Struct update syntax is an expression too, and it moves the fields that it fills in.
Two patterns that look alike.
A lone underscore, and an underscore followed by a letter.
Which one leaves the option usable afterwards?

lines.text: Only the single underscore. It binds nothing, so nothing moves.
An underscore-prefixed name is still a name... it takes the buffer.
Match on a reference, and the names under the pattern become references.
The compiler carries a default binding mode. It starts at move.
Pass an ampersand, and the binding becomes ref. Pass a mutable reference, and it becomes the mutable ref.
And there's no way back from ref.
So matching on a reference moves nothing. This is match ergonomics.

A placeholder can't tell drop that the buffer is already gone, so the pool fills up with empty buffers.
Manually drop needs unsafe. None says exactly what happened, and here it costs nothing. Its price is a run-time check in each accessor.
Six things to keep.
Moving a field out leaves a hole, and the remaining fields are still dropped.
A type with a destructor is sealed.
Through a borrow, you never leave a hole. So take, replace and swap put one back.
A guard that hands its contents out keeps them in an option.
And every pattern binding moves, copies, or borrows.
The pooled buffer guard holds the pool by exclusive borrow, so only one guard can exist at a time.
